actions.name: FAST stroke screen (Face-Arm-Speech-Time) via video
actions.result: Face: obvious right-sided facial droop with asymmetric smile. Arm: right arm drifts downward within 10 seconds of holding both arms out, eyes closed. Speech: slurred, mildly difficult to understand but words are appropriate. Time: symptom onset approximately 40 minutes ago per patient and wife. FAST screen POSITIVE.

actions.name: Establish time last known well
actions.result: Patient was last seen normal at breakfast; wife states she was pouring his coffee when his hand went weak and face appeared crooked, about 40 minutes before this call. Time last known well charted as the time of symptom onset.

actions.name: Home blood pressure reading (patient's own cuff)
actions.result: 178/102 mmHg, right arm, seated, taken 10 minutes ago.

actions.name: Heart rate / pulse check (patient palpates or home device)
actions.result: Pulse 96 bpm, irregular rhythm reported by patient and confirmed by wife feeling his wrist.

actions.name: Camera inspection of face at rest and with smile
actions.result: Right nasolabial fold flattened, right corner of mouth droops with attempted smile; forehead wrinkles symmetrically (consistent with central, not peripheral, facial weakness).

actions.name: Arm drift test on camera (hold both arms out, eyes closed, 10 seconds)
actions.result: Right arm drifts downward and pronates within 10 seconds; left arm holds steady.

actions.name: Speech sample / repeat a sentence on camera
actions.result: Slurred, dysarthric speech noted; patient able to generate the sentence with effort, no clear word-finding difficulty reported.

actions.name: Grip strength comparison (ask patient to squeeze wife's hands, both sides)
actions.result: Right-hand grip clearly weaker than left per wife's report.

actions.name: Review problem list and medication list in chart
actions.result: Problem list: atrial fibrillation, hypertension. Medication list shows apixaban 5 mg twice daily and amlodipine 10 mg daily listed as active, with no refill alerts flagged in the chart itself. Pulling the pharmacy refill history (see attached) for cross-check: last apixaban fill was 37 days ago, a 30-day supply, with no refill logged since.

actions.name: Review last clinic visit note
actions.result: Visit 3 months ago: BP 148/88, AFib rate-controlled, apixaban continued for stroke prophylaxis, counseled on adherence.

actions.name: Confirm transport plan and distance to nearest stroke-capable hospital
actions.result: Nearest hospital with stroke/CT capability is approximately 35 minutes by private vehicle; patient initially wants to wait for Monday clinic appointment.

actions.name: Respiratory rate and temperature check
actions.result: Respiratory rate 18/min, non-labored. Temperature 98.4°F (36.9°C) per home thermometer, afebrile.

cells: Active - prescribed for AFib stroke prevention

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient initially frames his anticoagulant use as current ('I take a pill for that too' / only reveals lapse when asked directly), and the 3-month-old clinic note documents he reported taking apixaban without missed doses
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows the last apixaban fill was 37 days ago (a 30-day supply), meaning the medication ran out about 7 days ago with no refill since, confirming an actual lapse in anticoagulation despite his routine self-report at the last visit of 'no missed doses'
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence can be inaccurate or outdated; pharmacy refill data is an objective adherence check, and a lapsed anticoagulant in a patient with atrial fibrillation substantially raises stroke risk and urgency - this reinforces, but does not change, the triage decision to activate EMS now.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient minimizes the event as having 'slept on his arm wrong' and views it as not serious enough to warrant an ambulance
mismatches.recordEvidence: Home blood pressure log shows a clear upward trend over the preceding two weeks (142/86 to 178/102 today) with pulse rising concurrently, objective evidence of worsening, poorly controlled hypertension in an anticoagulation-lapsed AFib patient - a high-risk substrate for acute stroke that the patient's own framing does not reflect
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may rationalize new focal neurologic symptoms as benign; triage nurses must rely on objective findings (FAST screen, vital trends) rather than the patient's own interpretation to drive the acuity decision.

objectives.text: Rapidly recognize signs of acute stroke (facial droop, arm drift, slurred speech) using a FAST-based remote screening approach via video
Establish and document an accurate time last known well as a critical data point for emergency transport and treatment eligibility
Correctly assign the highest triage acuity level and activate emergency medical services immediately rather than deferring to a routine clinic appointment
Elicit and reconcile a mismatch between patient self-report of medication adherence and objective pharmacy/record evidence, recognizing lapsed anticoagulation as a major stroke risk factor
Provide correct protocol-based safety instructions for a suspected stroke: nothing by mouth, do not give aspirin, remain on the line, prepare for EMS arrival
Address patient and family barriers (cost concern, reluctance to 'make a fuss', distance to hospital) with empathetic, firm communication while maintaining the emergency plan

scenario.studentBrief: You are an emergency triage nurse answering a call to the nurse line. The caller is Earl Jackson, 71, who reports his right hand went clumsy and he dropped his coffee cup about 40 minutes ago; he says his words are coming out a little strange and his wife, in the background, says his face looks crooked. He wants to know if he can just wait and see his regular doctor on Monday. Conduct a focused remote assessment, assign an acuity level, and give protocol-based instructions.

scenario.openingLine: Hi, this is Earl Jackson calling. My right hand just quit working right and I dropped my coffee cup about forty minutes ago. I figure I just slept on it wrong, but my wife's fussing at me to call. Can I just wait and see my regular doctor Monday?
tasks: Perform a rapid remote stroke screen via video
Establish and document the time of symptom onset

Review the patient's current medications and adherence
Provide clear instructions and address the patient's and family's questions

profile.summary: "This case simulates a nurse tele-triage call for a 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation and hypertension who develops sudden right-sided facial droop, arm drift, and slurred speech after a one-week lapse in anticoagulation, requiring immediate recognition of acute stroke, correct highest-acuity triage, and EMS activation despite the patient's minimization and preference to wait for a routine appointment. It teaches FAST-based remote stroke screening, time-last-known-well documentation, protocol-based safety instructions (NPO, no aspirin), and reconciling patient self-report with objective record evidence (pharmacy refill history, home BP trend)."

answerKey.primaryProblem: Acute ischemic stroke (suspected), highest triage acuity requiring immediate EMS activation
differential: Acute ischemic stroke (most likely given FAST-positive findings, lapsed anticoagulation in AFib, and acute onset)
Hemorrhagic stroke (cannot be distinguished from ischemic without imaging; equally emergent)
Transient ischemic attack (cannot be assumed prospectively; must be treated as stroke until proven otherwise)
Hypoglycemia with focal neurologic symptoms (less likely, no diabetes history, but reasonable to consider if glucometer were available)
Bell's palsy (less likely given concurrent arm drift, speech change, and forehead sparing pattern consistent with central not peripheral weakness)
keyFindings: Acute onset (~40 minutes) right facial droop, right arm drift, and dysarthria - FAST positive
History of atrial fibrillation with a 7-day lapse in apixaban, markedly increasing stroke risk
Elevated blood pressure 178/102 with an escalating 2-week home BP trend
New right-sided visual blurring and mouth/swallowing dysfunction with drooling
Patient minimizing symptoms and wishing to defer care to a routine Monday appointment
plan: Assign highest triage acuity (Level 1/emergent) and activate emergency medical services immediately - do not advise patient to drive himself or wait for a scheduled appointment
Clearly document and communicate the time last known well to EMS and receiving facility
Instruct patient to remain nothing by mouth (NPO) given swallowing/mouth weakness and drooling, to reduce aspiration risk
Instruct patient NOT to take aspirin or any medication, given uncertain stroke type (ischemic vs hemorrhagic) and that this determination requires imaging at the hospital
Stay on the line with patient and wife until EMS arrives; reassess airway, breathing, level of consciousness, and any symptom progression while waiting
Complete and hand off a structured SBAR to EMS/receiving ED including FAST findings, time last known well, vital signs, anticoagulation lapse, and home BP trend

Address cost and transport concerns empathetically but firmly: explain that time-sensitive treatment options for stroke are only available with rapid EMS transport to a stroke-capable hospital, and that delay directly worsens outcomes
Explicitly reassure patient and wife that this is not 'making a fuss' - this is a time-critical emergency - without being dismissive of their very real financial worries
Hand off medical decision-making (e.g., whether to resume/hold apixaban, any imaging or clot-directed therapy) to the receiving emergency physician/stroke team; this is outside triage nurse scope
redFlags: Sudden onset focal neurologic deficit (facial droop, arm weakness, slurred speech) - treat as stroke until proven otherwise
Known atrial fibrillation with recent anticoagulation lapse - high embolic stroke risk
New swallowing difficulty/drooling - aspiration risk, reinforces NPO instruction
Patient and family minimization or desire to delay care in the face of objective emergent findings
educationPoints: FAST (Face, Arm, Speech, Time) is a validated, rapid screen that can be performed remotely via video and should prompt immediate EMS activation when positive, regardless of symptom severity as perceived by the patient
Time last known well is a critical, time-stamped data point that determines eligibility for time-sensitive stroke therapies at the receiving hospital and must be clearly established and documented

Aspirin and other medications should not be given for suspected stroke before imaging, because hemorrhagic stroke cannot be distinguished from ischemic stroke by symptoms alone and aspirin could worsen a hemorrhage

Lapsed anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation substantially raises embolic stroke risk and should be flagged and relayed to receiving clinicians, but adjusting or restarting anticoagulation is outside triage nursing scope
Objective data (pharmacy refill records, home BP/vital trends, standardized screens) should be used to validate or challenge a patient's self-report, especially when a patient minimizes symptoms
Empathetic, non-judgmental communication about cost and family dynamics can improve adherence to urgent recommendations without compromising the clinical decision
